title: Predictive prefetch + deferred operator-fusion and neighborhood sharding: proposal
content:
Summary:

This doc proposes a complementary set of runtime techniques aimed at reducing wall-clock latency and cross-GPU bandwidth for large-context, multi-GPU serving workloads. The three ideas are designed to work together but are independently deployable: (1) predictive prefetch for KV cache entries to reduce cold misses, (2) deferred operator-fusion that groups small elementwise / reduction kernels to amortize kernel launch overhead and PCIe/NCCL staging, and (3) neighborhood sharding, a partial KV placement strategy that keeps hot KV segments replicated within small GPU neighborhoods to trade off memory for reduced inter-node collectives.

Goals and motivation:
- Reduce tail token latency (p99/p995) for interactive requests with large context windows.
- Cut cross-node NCCL traffic for common short-step token generation patterns.
- Reduce CPU/GPU kernel launch overhead for chat-style bursty traffic.
- Keep end-to-end quality and deterministic behavior for pinned model versions.

High-level approach:
1) Predictive prefetch (lightweight predictor):
   - Observe per-route token transition patterns (tokens, top-k next token indices, or compressed token n-grams) and maintain a tiny LRU predictor per serving route (bounded memory).
   - On each generation step, use predictor to schedule KV prefetches for KV partitions likely to be referenced in the next N=1..4 steps. Prefetch is best-effort and cancellable.
   - Prefetch priority is weighted by request latency sensitivity (route tier) and predictor confidence.
   - Integrates with existing prefix/KV cache: prefetch populates local GPU cache or local neighborhood shadow asynchronously.

   Rationale: Many production chat/assistant flows are dominated by a small set of next-token transitions (system tokens, templated completions). Lightweight predictors can capture those and avoid expensive on-demand NCCL transfers.

2) Deferred operator-fusion (deferred-opfusion):
   - Collect small GPU operators produced during the token step (layer-norm + add + gelu-ish small ops, small matrix transposes, broadcast adds) into a deferred buffer for the step window.
   - At a short timeout boundary (e.g., 150-300 microseconds) fuse these into a single custom kernel or a small number of fused kernels using precompiled templates (no JIT at runtime; uses a small set of tiled templates tuned for common shapes).
   - If fusion timeout expires or buffered work exceeds threshold, flush immediately.
   - Fusion targets: elementwise chains, small reductions, and KV pack/unpack ops that currently cause multiple kernels and synchronization points.

   Rationale: On multi-tenant inference nodes with many small requests, kernel launch overhead and PCIe/NCCL staging for many tiny tensors dominates. Deferred fusion amortizes that cost and improves device utilization. The short timeout bounds additional latency introduced by batching.

3) Neighborhood sharding (partial KV replication):
   - Replace strict full-sharding with a tiered placement: each KV partition has a primary owner and a small neighborhood group (size M=2..4 GPUs) that keep warm copies of the recent KV slices.
   - Neighborhood groups are topology-aware (same NVLink domain or same host first, then rack-local). When a request's KV lookup resolves to a partition, the runtime first checks local neighborhood, then falls back to primary fetch if missing.
   - Periodic asynchronous reconciliation ensures that neighborhood copies are eventually consistent for cold segments; warm segments receive continuous updates.
   - Reduce cross-host NCCL allgather/alltoall by serving a large fraction of requests inside neighborhoods (localized collectives or host-local memory copies).

   Rationale: Many workloads hit a small subset of KV entries repeatedly; fully sharded KV causes cross-node collectives even for hot entries. Neighborhood sharding opportunistically replicates hot entries closer to where requests run.

NCCL and network tuning notes:
- Use staggered asynchronous collectives: schedule high-priority small-message transfers first using NCCL group primitives but stagger the larger alltoall work to reduce head-of-line blocking on rings.
- Prioritize within NCCL by tagging requests: urgent interactive steps use prioritized CUDA streams and pinned buffers; background bulk updates use lower-priority streams and can be bandwidth-throttled at runtime.
- Experiment with in-node host staging using NVLINK peer direct copies (cudaMemcpyPeerAsync) for neighborhood hits vs full NCCL collective for cross-node; benchmark threshold where peer copies outperform collectives depending on message size and topology.

Integration sketches / control flow pseudocode:
- On token generation request arrival:
  1. route -> select model partition placement -> local worker enqueues step.
  2. predictor.predict(next_token_context) -> list of KV segment ids with confidence.
  3. async_prefetch(segments, priority) -> attempts local/neighborhood fetch first.
  4. build operator DAG for step; instead of immediate kernel launches, push small ops into deferred buffer.
  5. if deferred buffer flush condition met -> run fused kernel(s); else schedule deferred flush at short timeout.
  6. when kernels produce KV writes (new activations), write-through to local cache and fan-out to neighborhood asynchronously.

Experiment matrix (initial 8-week plan):
- Week 0-1: microbench predictive prefetch offline simulation using production traces (1M steps); measure prefetch hit rate for N=1..4 and memory cost. Success: >60% hit for N=1 on top-10 routes.
- Week 2-3: implement predictive prefetch prototype (no replication) + tracer hooks, run on canary fleet (5 nodes). Measure p50/p95/p99 token latency, CPU/GPU utilization, and added memory.
- Week 4-5: implement deferred-opfusion templates and benchmark with synthetic microbatch shapes. Success: reduce per-step kernel launches by 30% and reduce p50 latency by 10-15% on small-shot traffic.
- Week 6: combine prefetch + deferred-opfusion on canary; compare against baseline.
- Week 7-8: neighborhood shard prototype (M=2) with topology-aware placement; measure reduction in cross-host NCCL bytes and tail latency.

Metrics and targets:
- p99 token latency improvement: target 15-30% for interactive routes.
- Cross-node NCCL bytes: target reduction 30-60% for warm-state workloads.
- Memory overhead (neighborhood shadow): target < 10% increase in GPU memory for M=2 and hot-only replication.
- CPU overhead (predictor): < 2% CPU per serving core.

Risks and mitigations:
- Predictor misfires: can cause wasted bandwidth. Mitigation: conservative thresholds and ability to disable per-route; track per-route prefetch precision and fall back to baseline if precision < 40%.
- Consistency concerns with neighborhood replication: must ensure correctness for read-after-write sequences; mitigation: write-through semantics where synchronous writes still update primary and local worker; asynchronous neighborhood updates carry causal version stamps and readers can fall back to primary for exact reads if needed.
- Increased memory pressure: mitigate by tracking per-segment hotness and dynamically evicting neighborhood copies.
- Complexity and debugging difficulty: expose observability hooks (prefetch telemetry, deferred buffer stats, neighborhood hit/miss logs).

Open questions and decisions required:
- Predictor features: raw token ids vs compressed token class embeddings? Tradeoffs in CPU cost and memory.
- Default neighborhood size M and placement policy for multi-host racks.
- Fusion template coverage: which small operators to prioritize first? (LN->add->gelu, KV pack/unpack, transpose chains)
- Failure modes for prioritized NCCL streams on heterogeneous hardware; coordinate with SRE on fallback policies.

Action items:
- Aisha: run offline prefetch sims on last 30 days of traces (INF-6124).
- Marco: prototype deferred-opfusion template for LN+add+GELU and benchmark kernel latency improvements.
- Diego: topology-aware neighborhood placement prototype; instrument NCCL counters and cross-host bytes.
- Priya: wire up observability events and define canary plan for combination rollout.

Appendix: lightweight predictor sketch:
- Data: maintain counts of (previous token hash -> next token id) and top-3 successors per context signature (context signature is hashed last K tokens and route id).
- Memory: 8k signature table per route, 3 successors each, approx 64KB per hot route. Evict LRU.
- Update: online counting with decayed counters to adapt to shifting semantics.

Notes: This proposal leans toward opportunistic optimization with fallbacks. Each component can be gated and rolled out independently. The biggest wins for tail latency are expected when all three are enabled together on chatbot routes that have stable next-token patterns.
